A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSN and brain-decoding research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across reorganization and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original SSN experiments on brain-stimulus classification, traffic-flow regression and node classification, including additional empirical analyses in Appendix I.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds topological-feature SVM comparisons, attention-based experiments and training-runtime results.

M1.justification: The SSN update, routing mechanism and auxiliary loss, DAC construction, and traffic-regression objective remain unchanged. The newly evaluated GAT implementation instantiates an option already explicitly supported in v1 Appendix F.1.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same brain-classification tasks, four traffic datasets, and Cora-ML, Citeseer and Roman-Empire. Higher temporal resolution, smaller brain volumes and non-invariant readouts already appear in v1. The explicit 'four tasks across 13 datasets' summary does not establish expanded coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds TopoFeat+SVM to all six primary brain comparisons and evaluates GAT, Dir-GAT and MPSNN-GAT against SSN-GAT in Table 8. This substantially expands comparison beyond the original neural baselines to handcrafted topological features and attention-based alternatives. Existing comparison methods are retained.

E3.justification: New evaluations vary the SVM neighborhood order over K=1,2,3, use GAT message passing on the retained (4,325µm) and M=3 settings, and measure training time per epoch. Existing split ratios, hyperparameter grids and task-specific protocols remain substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds targeted checks of sensitivity to SVM neighborhood order and whether SSN's advantage persists with attention-based messages. It also extends runtime analysis to training costs across complex sizes. The earlier readout, temporal-resolution, volumetric and graph-directionality analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across five brain-data splits and ten splits for Cora-ML/Citeseer. Runtime uncertainty already appears in v1 Table 4. Additional result rows continue existing reporting practices; no changed run counts, seed policies or statistical estimation procedures are reported.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial numerical evidence from TopoFeat+SVM, neighborhood-order comparisons, attention experiments and training runtimes. For example, SSN-GAT achieves 77.45±3.58 and 51.27±1.85 in Table 8. Previously reported brain, traffic and node results remain unchanged; these additions are not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v3 adds formal definitions distinguishing orientation from directionality and defining n-uniform relations. Appendix G.4 corrects Lemma 7's higher-order-directionality example from {1,1,0,0} to {1,1,-1,-1}. The principal expressivity, equivariance, invariant-recovery and complexity results remain, with mostly explanatory proof revisions.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain SSNs and routing, stronger expressivity, DAC-based recovery of neurotopological invariants, and superior brain-stimulus classification with competitive additional benchmarks. Revised wording and the explicit task/dataset count restate the existing scope.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the SVM comparisons as evidence favoring learned representations over predefined invariants. It also qualifies routing's efficiency: gating overhead can outweigh savings on small complexes, including slightly slower training. The earlier limitations concerning directionality mismatch and unavailable in-vivo connectomic information are retained.

D1.justification: v1 promises future code and data release; v3 Section 7 supplies concrete GitHub and Zenodo access addresses. v3 also explicitly identifies experimental relation choices and documents the SVM feature construction, aggregation and parameter counts. These materially strengthen reproducibility information without establishing changes to the retained implementation.

R1.justification: v3 expands the comparison between combinatorial complexes and semi-simplicial sets, stating that neither framework subsumes the other. It adds relevant citations including relational WL, copresheaf networks, higher-order human connectomics and GAT. The overall positioning relative to directed simplicial learning and neurotopology remains.

P1.justification: Much of the main text is rewritten, with reordered preliminaries, more concrete examples and expanded explanations of directionality and invariants. Reproducibility moves into the main text, and the experimental appendix is reorganized into clearer subsections. These are extensive narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: v3 substantially revises the visual presentation: Figure 2 becomes a four-panel domain comparison, and Figure 3 brings existing appendix relation/path illustrations into the main text. Table 3 gains the SVM row, the runtime table expands to validation and training panels, and new Tables 7–8 present supplementary comparisons. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens the existing study with a directly relevant handcrafted-feature baseline, attention-based controls, more informative efficiency analysis, clearer exposition and concrete code/data access information. These provide useful validation and reproducibility gains. A small reporting problem offsets some benefit: the new TopoFeat+SVM entries in Tables 3 and 7 disagree, including the (4,325µm) standard deviation and the M=1 result associated with the stated K=3 configuration.
